'''Richard J. "Dick" Cannings''' (born March 31, 1954) is a [[Canadians|Canadian]] [[biologist]], author and politician. He was elected as the [[South Okanagan—West Kootenay]] [[Member of Parliament (Canada)|Member of Parliament]] in the [[2015 Canadian federal election]] for the [[New Democratic Party]], and re-elected in 2019 and 2021. He did not run for re-election in 2025. As a member of the [[42nd Canadian Parliament]] he sponsored three [[private member's bill#Canada|private member's bills]]: one to promote the use of wood in federal public works projects, one to add various lakes and rivers to ''Navigable Waters Protection Act'', and another to a [[Minister of Environment and Climate Change (Canada)|Minister of Environment]] to respond to a [[Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada]] report. Cannings was appointed the NDP Critic for Post-Secondary Education as well as the Deputy Critic for [[Minister of Natural Resources (Canada)|Natural Resources]] in the [[42nd Canadian Parliament]].<ref name="NDP 42nd Critics">{{cite news | url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/ndp-critics-list-mulcair-thursday-1.3315431 | title=Tom Mulcair taps Nathan Cullen, Charlie Angus, Guy Caron for top critic roles | publisher=[[The Canadian Press]] | work=[[CBC News]] | date=12 November 2015 | access-date=12 November 2015 | author=Kirkup, Kristy}}</ref> He became the NDP Critic for Natural Resources in 2016 and served in that position until 2021. In October 2021, he became the NDP Critic for Emergency Preparedness (Climate Adaptation) and Critic for Small Business and Tourism, as well as Deputy Critic for Natural Resources and Deputy Critic for Innovation, Science and Industry. In December 2021, he was named an inaugural member of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Science and Research.

Prior to being elected as a member of parliament, Cannings unsuccessfully sought election as a [[Legislative Assembly of British Columbia|member of the legislative assembly]] of British Columbia in the [[2013 British Columbia general election|2013 BC election]]. Prior to his involvement in politics, Cannings worked as a biologist specializing in birds, taught at the [[University of British Columbia]] for 17 years, wrote numerous books about birds and [[natural history]], and was a member of the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada for 8 years. He is an alumnus of [[Memorial University of Newfoundland]] and the University of British Columbia.

==Career==
Like their father, renowned environmentalist Stephen Cannings, Richard and his twin brother Sydney and their older brother, Rob, were born and raised in Penticton and all pursued careers in biology.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pentictonherald.ca/news/article_3a123a22-70ee-11e7-96e9-d7ebca5c588f.html |publisher=[[Penticton Herald]] |title=Stephen Cannings was one of the South Okanagan's greatest environmentalists |date= July 24, 2017 |access-date=July 27, 2019 |first=Joyce |last=Langerak}}</ref> Richard earned a master's degree in [[zoology]] from [[Memorial University of Newfoundland]]. He taught for 17 years at University of British Columbia before returning to Penticton in 1995 to work as a consulting biologist, including doing work for the non-profit [[Bird Studies Canada]]. He spent 8 years on the [[Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada]] as co-chair for Birds, 11 years on B.C. Environmental Appeal Board and five on the B.C. Forest Appeals Commission.<ref>{{cite news |title=Fresh face aims to enlighten them with science |last=Bitonti |first=Daniel |newspaper=[[The Globe and Mail]] |date=May 2, 2013 |page=S3}}</ref> He was a board member of the [[Nature Conservancy of Canada]] from 2006 to 2015.

Cannings authored or contributed to numerous books. In 1987 he co-authored with his brothers ''Birds of the Okanagan Valley, British Columbia'' which was published by the [[Royal British Columbia Museum]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Birds of the Okanagan Valley, British Columbia |first1= Robert A |last1=Cannings |first2=Richard J |last2=Cannings |first3=Sydney G |last3=Cannings |publisher=[[Royal British Columbia Museum]] |location=[[Victoria, British Columbia]] |year=1987 |isbn=9780771886010}}</ref> Based on previous work, he co-authored ''Birds of Southwestern British Columbia''<ref>{{cite book |title=Birds of Southwestern British Columbia |first1= Richard |last1=Cannings |first2=Hal |last2=Opperman |first3=Tom |last3=Aversa |publisher=Heritage House Publishing |location=[[Victoria, British Columbia]] |year=2005 |isbn=9781894974592}}</ref> and ''Birds of Interior BC and the Rockies''<ref>{{cite book |title=Birds of Interior BC and the Rockies |first1= Richard |last1=Cannings |first2=Harry B. |last2=Nehls|first3=Dave |last3=Trochlell |first4=Mike |last4=Denny |publisher=Heritage House Publishing |location=[[Victoria, British Columbia]] |year=2009 |isbn=9781894974592}}</ref> In 2007 [[Greystone Books]] published a memoir style book of essays by Cannings titled ''An Enchantment of Birds: Memories From A Birder's Life''<ref>{{cite news |title=A Birder's Life: The Wonder of it All |newspaper=[[The Hamilton Spectator]] |location= [[Hamilton, Ontario]] |date=December 1, 2007 |page=D14}}</ref> and in 2010 Greystone published a book of essays, titled ''Flights of Imagination: Extraordinary Writing about Birds'', edited by Cannings.<ref>{{cite news |title=Cheep thrills Books for bird-watchers |last=Boodman |first= Eric |newspaper=[[Ottawa Citizen]] |location= [[Ottawa|Ottawa, Ontario]] |date=May 23, 2010 |page=A8}}</ref> Co-authored with his son Russell, Cannings contributed to ''Birdfinding in British Columbia'' and ''Best Places to Bird in British Columbia'', both also published by Greystone.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/best-birdwatching-1.4113785 |title=New book reveals best places for B.C. birdwatching |first1=Bridgette |last1=Watson |date=May 14, 2017 |access-date=July 30, 2019 |publisher= [[CBC News]]}}</ref>

==Politics==
At 58 years old, Cannings entered politics in 2012 seeking the [[British Columbia New Democratic Party]] nomination in [[Penticton (electoral district)|Penticton]]. Cannings won the nomination over [[Summerland, British Columbia|Summerland]] councillor David Finnis.<ref>{{cite news |title= NDP will nominate Penticton candidate on Sunday |newspaper=Penticton Western News |location=[[Penticton]], BC |date=November 15, 2012 |page=8}}</ref> However, in the [[2013 British Columbia general election|2013 election]], Cannings lost to Penticton mayor [[Dan Ashton]] of the [[British Columbia Liberal Party|BC Liberal Party]], which went on to form a majority government with the BC NDP as the official opposition.

Cannings continued with politics by seeking the federal NDP nomination in [[South Okanagan—West Kootenay]]. He won the nomination over Margaret Maximenko of [[Christina Lake, British Columbia|Christina Lake]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Penticton candidate seeks NDP role |newspaper=Trail Times |location=[[Trail, British Columbia]] |date=January 15, 2014 |page=A3}}</ref> In the [[2015 Canadian federal election|2015 election]], Cannings won the riding with 37% of the vote.<ref>{{cite news |last=Fries |first=Joe |date=October 17, 2019 |title=NDP Leader Singh returning to Penticton |url=https://www.pentictonherald.ca/news/article_9828b9e2-f0fd-11e9-8362-4fc4b53ed383.html |work=[[Penticton Herald]] |location=Penticton, British Columbia |access-date=December 4, 2023}}</ref> Nationally, the NDP placed third with the Liberal Party forming a majority government.<ref>{{cite news |last=Blackwell |first=Tom |date=October 20, 2015 |title=Canadian election 2015 hands Justin Trudeau and the Liberals a majority government |url=https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/canadian-election-2015-liberals-jump-to-early-lead-as-polls-close-in-newfoundland-and-labrador |work=[[National Post]] |location= |access-date=December 4, 2023}}</ref>

During ensuing [[42nd Canadian Parliament|42nd Parliament]] Cannings was appointed by NDP leader [[Thomas Mulcair]] as their critic on post-secondary education issues and deputy critic of natural resources under [[Carol Hughes (politician)|Carol Hughes]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Cannings officially sworn in at the Hill |last=Boyd |first= Dale |newspaper=Penticton Western News |location=[[Penticton]], BC |date=November 26, 2015}}</ref> He became critic of natural resources in 2016 when [[Carol Hughes (politician)|Carol Hughes]] was named Assistant Deputy Speaker, and he served the entire Parliament on the [[Canadian House of Commons Standing Committee on Natural Resources|Standing Committee on Natural Resources]]. Cannings sponsored three private member bills. On April 13, 2017, he introduced Bill C-354 which would amend the ''Public Works and Government Services Act'' which would promote the use of wood in federal public works projects. Similar bills had previously been introduced by [[Claude Patry]] and [[Gérard Asselin]] in the [[41st Canadian Parliament|41st]] and [[40th Canadian Parliament|40th]] Parliaments, respectively. The bill was passed by the House of Commons with support from all parties except the Conservative Party but was blocked from proceeding in the Senate by the Conservatives.<ref>{{cite news |title=Richard Cannings: How my private member's bill died in the Senate |last=Nesteroff |first=Greg |newspaper=Castlegar News |location=[[Castlegar, British Columbia]] |date=July 6, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/dozens-of-bills-including-on-sexual-assault-and-undrip-die-in-senate-amid-conservative-filibuster |title=Dozens of bills, including on sexual assault and UNDRIP, die in Senate amid Conservative filibuster |newspaper=[[National Post]] |date=June 20, 2019 |access-date=July 27, 2019 |first=Marie-Danielle |last=Smith}}</ref> In response to the [[41st Canadian Parliament|previous parliament]]'s ''[[Jobs and Growth Act]]'', Cannings second private member bill, Bill C-360, sought to re-insert several lakes and rivers such as [[Skaha Lake]], [[Vaseux Lake]], [[Tuc-el-nuit Lake]], [[Osoyoos Lake]], [[Christina Lake (British Columbia)|Christina Lake]], [[Okanagan River]], [[Slocan River]], [[Kettle River (Columbia River tributary)|Kettle River]], and [[Granby River]] back into the ''[[Navigation Protection Act|Navigable Waters Protection Act]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/42-1/bill/C-360/first-reading |title=Bill C-360 An Act to amend the Navigation Protection Act (certain lakes and rivers in British Columbia) |access-date=July 28, 2019 |date=April 14, 2017 |publisher=Parliament of Canada}}</ref> However, Bill C-360 did not advance past first reading as the government bill C-69 was amending the same act to re-define what water bodies and watercourses are deemed to be reviewable as navigable waters. He introduced his third private member bill, Bill C-363,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/42-1/bill/C-363/first-reading |title=Bill C-363 An Act to amend the Species at Risk Act (amendment of the List) |access-date=July 31, 2019 |date=September 22, 2017 |publisher=Parliament of Canada}}</ref> on September 22, 2017, as a response to the practice used by the [[Minister of Environment and Climate Change (Canada)|Ministers of Environment]] in the [[28th Canadian Ministry]] between 2011 and 2015 of avoiding listing species in the Species at risk Public Registry by not notifying the Governor in Council of reports received from the [[Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada]]. Though Bill C-363, which would require the Minister notify the Governor in Council and recommend to list a species or not, did not advance but it was adopted as a Ministry of Environment operational policy.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://thenarwhal.ca/it-just-takes-too-damn-long-how-canadas-law-for-protecting-at-risk-species-is-failing/ |publisher=The Narwhal |title='It just takes too damn long': How Canada's law for protecting at-risk species is failing |first=Larry |last=Pinn |date=April 18, 2019 |access-date=July 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Returning Species at Risk Act to original intent |last=Cannings |first=Richard |newspaper=Trail Times |location=[[Trail, British Columbia]] |date=September 27, 2017 |page=A6}}</ref>

In the [[2019 Canadian federal election]], Cannings was narrowly re-elected over the second-place Conservative, Penticton city councillor [[Helena Konanz]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.pentictonwesternnews.com/news/konanz-issues-challenge-to-south-okanagan-west-kootenay-candidates/ |title=Konanz issues challenge to South Okanagan-West Kootenay candidates |date=July 30, 2019 |access-date=August 5, 2019 |publisher=Penticton Western News |first= Kristi |last=Patton}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.pentictonherald.ca/news/article_9e26a7f8-f492-11e9-87b1-37ace612dab9.html|title= ELECTION 2019: Cannings preserves seat|date= October 21, 2019}}</ref> He was again re-elected in the [[2021 Canadian federal election|2021 federal election]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Potenteau |first=Doyle |date=September 12, 2023 |title=Okanagan politician Richard Cannings not seeking federal re-election in 2025 |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/9956111/richard-cannings-not-seeking-federal-re-election/ |work=[[Global News]] |location= |access-date=December 4, 2023}}</ref>

In September 2023, Cannings announced he would not seek re-election in the [[2025 Canadian federal election|2025 federal election]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Fries|first=Joe |date=September 12, 2023 |title=MP Cannings won't run again |url=https://www.pentictonherald.ca/news/article_4185cf98-519e-11ee-92fc-cffcf6976c79.html |work=Penticton Herald |location= |access-date=December 4, 2023}}</ref>

Cannings endorsed Alberta MP [[Heather McPherson (politician)|Heather McPherson]] in the [[2026 New Democratic Party leadership election]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pentictonherald.ca/news/article_e15f3ef6-79a6-43ab-8195-59065f1c1ee4.html|title=Cannings endorses Heather McPherson|website=[[Penticton Herald]] |date=November 14, 2025 }}</ref>
